newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen firm in Europe after G7 Summit.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen firm in Europe after G7 Summit.

text.p: The dollar motored more than one yen higher in early Europe to peaks around 115.67 yen in the wake of the G7 summit, which downplayed US-Japan trade friction and generally broke little new ground, said analysts.

"Basically, they (G7) downplayed trade friction between the U.S. and Japan and instead the U.S. put the emphasis on increased deregulation by Japanese authorities," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
Markets had been expecting the U.S. to use the G7 meeting in Denver, which ended on Sunday, as a platform to target Japan's ballooning trade surplus with the U.S.

At 0730 GMT, dollar/yen was firm at 115.20 yen but off session highs around 115.67 yen though well up from late Friday levels around 114.51/56 yen. Dollar/mark, however, was steady to a touch weaker, trading at 1.7280/85 marks against 1.7295/00 in late Europe and session peaks of 1.7320 marks hit earlier.

G7 nations in a joint statement at the end of the meeting said Japan needs to spur strong domestic demand-led growth, avoid significant increase in its external surplus, deregulate and enact structural fiscal reforms.
"This has come as a relief to the market and consequently the dollar has benefited," said DKB's Stamenkovic.

The statement, issued at the end of the two-day meeting on Sunday, also asked finance ministers of G7 nations - Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the U.S. - to continue close cooperation on economic policy and financial markets.

The summit leaders said the global economy was in good shape, but warned that there may be problems ahead. The final communique also expressed concern over the high unemployment in continental Europe and said the U.S must prevent its booming economy spinning into inflation.
With the G7 summit now over, currency markets will focus on Japan ahead of the release of the Tankan report, said analysts.
"The dollar is looking forward to a soft Tankan. But I think that is largely discounted by the Japanese money markets," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He said, however, the dollar was likely to remain well bid in the run-up to the Tankan.
"But we could well see a 'buy on the rumour, sell the fact' response," he added.
A weak Tankan, said Meggyesi, would confirm expectations currently embedded in Japanese currency markets.
